DeepAgents (source_001) is built on LangGraph and bundles planning, sub-agents, a filesystem abstraction, and HITL controls, but in v0.1 its autonomous planning and dynamic sub-agent generation are disabled, so it functions as a fixed-DAG harness. That matches the router's per-node model-selection focus (source_005) and keeps the routing logic deterministic.

LangGraph (source_002) is the lower-level execution substrate: explicit nodes/edges, durable state, and check-pointing. The tradeoff is flexibility-versus-control: it provides the primitives DeepAgents composes, but lacks the higher-level planner/HITL ergonomics, so using it directly increases engineering effort for marginal control gains.

Pydantic AI (source_003) is not a v0.1 core dependency. Its typed tool definitions and structured outputs are valuable when schema validation becomes a bottleneck, but adopting it now adds API surface without addressing the routing objective. The pragmatic tradeoff is deferral: keep it as an optional validator layer once structured parsing demonstrably limits quality.

DeepSeek Harness (source_004) is reserved for the outer validation environment, not the core routing loop. RefractRouter v0.1 Platform Selection: DeepAgents, LangGraph, Pydantic AI, and DeepSeek Harness

Executive Summary

RefractRouter v0.1 adopts a layered stack: LangGraph as the execution substrate, DeepAgents on top as a fixed-DAG harness with autonomous planning disabled, Pydantic AI deferred as an optional structured-output layer, and DSH reserved for the outer validation environment [source_001][source_002][source_003][source_004]. This split keeps per-node model selection deterministic while isolating harness experimentation from router benchmarking [source_005][source_007].

Background

Most LLM routing research selects one model for an entire request; RefractRouter instead selects a model separately for each node in a task DAG to improve the quality-cost-latency Pareto frontier [source_005]. Static task decomposition is delegated to the application layer, so the router receives the DAG as input and focuses on per-node model selection [source_006]. This framing motivates a stack that emphasizes fixed-DAG execution over dynamic re-planning [source_005][source_006].

Selection Criteria

Candidate platforms were evaluated against four criteria: a fixed-DAG execution substrate, a plan and sub-agent control surface, structured-output tooling, and harness flexibility for outer validation [source_001][source_002][source_003][source_004]. The benchmark design further requires fixed task DAGs, per-node and per-task scoring, cost accounting, and critical-path latency, with a versioned rubric covering requirement coverage, evidence accuracy, analysis depth, structure, and HTML validity [source_007][source_008].

Platform Comparison

DeepAgents is a LangChain harness built on LangGraph that bundles planning, sub-agents, a filesystem abstraction, and HITL controls; in v0.1 its autonomous planning and dynamic sub-agent generation are disabled, so it acts as a fixed-DAG harness [source_001]. LangGraph is a graph state machine framework with explicit nodes, edges, durable state, and check-pointing, supplying the lower-level primitives that DeepAgents composes [source_002]. Pydantic AI offers typed tool definitions and structured outputs, useful when schema validation becomes a bottleneck, but it is not a v0.1 core dependency [source_003]. DeepSeek Harness treats the agent loop itself as a plugin and is reserved for the outer validation environment rather than the core routing loop [source_004].

Risks

Using LangGraph directly would increase engineering effort for marginal control gains over DeepAgents, since DeepAgents already supplies the needed fixed-DAG surface [source_001][source_002]. Adopting Pydantic AI in v0.1 enlarges the API surface without addressing per-node routing objectives, so premature integration is a maintainability risk [source_003]. Externalizing DSH preserves a clean internal-versus-external evaluation boundary but adds an extra moving part in the validation stack that must be versioned alongside scoring prompts and rubric versions [source_004][source_007][source_008].

Conclusion

The v0.1 platform split is coherent: LangGraph beneath, DeepAgents as the fixed-DAG harness on top, Pydantic AI deferred until structured parsing demonstrably limits quality, and DSH externalized for outer validation [source_001][source_002][source_003][source_004]. This aligns the candidate set with the routing objective and the benchmark requirements for quality, cost, and critical-path latency measurement [source_005][source_007][source_008].

References

Evidence for each claim is drawn from source_001 (DeepAgents), source_002 (LangGraph), source_003 (Pydantic AI), source_004 (DeepSeek Harness), source_005 (LLM routing research gap), source_006 (task decomposition boundary), source_007 (benchmark design), and source_008 (scoring rubric), whose full text and content hashes are preserved in the evidence list.

  • LangGraph: LangGraph is a graph state machine framework for complex workflows, supporting explicit nodes, edges, durable state, and check-pointing, and is used by RefractRouter as the lower-level execution substrate for a fixed task DAG.
  • Pydantic AI: Pydantic AI provides typed tool definitions and structured model outputs, useful when strict schemas are required, but it is not a core dependency for RefractRouter v0.1 unless structured-output parsing becomes a bottleneck.
  • DeepSeek Harness: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is an agent harness where the agent loop itself is a plugin; for RefractRouter v0.1, DSH is reserved for the outer validation environment and is not used for the core routing loop.
  • LLM routing research gap: Existing LLM routing work mostly selects one model for an entire request; RefractRouter studies whether selecting a model separately for each node in a task DAG can improve the quality-cost-latency Pareto frontier.

judge.rationale: The report is comprehensive and well-structured. Requirement coverage is full: all seven required sections (Executive Summary, Background, Selection Criteria, Platform Comparison, Risks, Conclusion, References) are present, plus an additional Source Trace section with content hashes. Evidence accuracy is high: all three expected claims are supported with correct source attribution, and inline citations use data-cite-source-id attributes consistently. Minor deduction because the 'quality' aspect of the benchmark claim is inferred from 'scoring' in source_007 rather than stated verbatim, and some citations in the Risks section (e.g., the claim that using LangGraph directly would increase engineering effort) go slightly beyond the frozen sources, which do not explicitly compare engineering effort. Analysis depth is strong: the report synthesizes the sources into a coherent layered architecture rationale, covers trade-offs, and identifies risks. Structure and readability are good with clear headings and logical flow, though the prose is dense in places. HTML validity is full: the document has a proper DOCTYPE, html/head/body structure, meta charset, title, and well-formed tags with matching anchors between citations and the source trace list.
